cards.title: Why Online Evaluation Matters
cards.teaser: Offline metrics measure what your model predicts on historical data. Online metrics measure what your model causes in the real world. The gap between those two things is where most ML deployment failures live.

runs.text: Every ML team runs offline evaluations before deployment: hold-out test sets, cross-validation, benchmark suites. These are necessary but not sufficient. Offline evaluation answers: "How does the model perform on data we have already seen?" Online evaluation answers: "What does the model do to user behavior on data we have not yet seen?"

The distinction matters because ML models operate in open-loop systems where the model's output influences future inputs. A recommendation model that surfaces more news about topic X will cause more clicks on topic X, which feeds back into future training data. Offline evaluation captures a static snapshot of a dynamic system.

items.text: Distribution shift.
Real traffic differs from historical data in ways your test set cannot capture — seasonality, user cohort changes, upstream feature drift.
Feedback loops.
Model outputs change user behavior, which changes future inputs. Test sets are blind to these dynamics.
Proxy metric misalignment.
Optimizing precision@10 in offline evaluation may increase click-through rate while decreasing session length — the metric you actually care about.
Interaction effects.
A model's performance depends on how it interacts with upstream rankers, UI surfaces, and user expectations that do not exist in test sets.

runs.text: Netflix's experimentation platform, described in their 2016 paper "Selecting the Best Artwork for Videos through A/B Testing," estimates that roughly 90% of ideas that improve offline metrics either have no measurable online effect or actively hurt online metrics. Online evaluation is the only arbiter of true model value.

The discipline of online evaluation exists precisely because offline evaluation is a necessary but insufficient gate. Shipping a model that wins offline without validating online is optimism masquerading as rigor.

Offline metrics tell you how good your model is at predicting past data. Online metrics tell you what your model actually does to real users. You need both because the first does not reliably predict the second.

cards.title: The Offline/Online Gap
cards.teaser: A model that beats the champion on every offline benchmark can lose the live A/B test. This is not a fluke — it is a systematic property of how offline metrics relate to business outcomes, and understanding the gap is the foundation of experimental ML practice.

runs.text: The offline/online gap is the divergence between a model's offline evaluation score and its observed effect on the metrics you care about in production. The gap has three main sources:

items.text: Proxy metric mismatch.

You optimize NDCG@10 because it is measurable offline, but users care about whether they complete a task. NDCG correlates with task completion most of the time, but not all of the time. The gap is the cost of the proxy.
Label bias.

Historical labels reflect the previous model's decisions. If the old model never showed certain items, those items have no positive labels even if users would have liked them. A new model that surfaces those items looks worse on the historical test set but may perform better online.
User adaptation.
Users adapt to model behavior over time. A model change that looks large in controlled offline evaluation may produce small online lift because users quickly adjust their behavior.

runs.text: Microsoft Research's work on web search evaluation ("Evaluating the Accuracy of Implicit Feedback from Clicks and Query Reformulations," Joachims et al.) quantifies this gap empirically: click-through rate improvements in offline simulation predict direction but overestimate magnitude of live improvements by a factor of 2-5x.

Practical consequence: when an offline evaluation shows a 2% improvement, expect 0.4%–1% online. Teams that do not account for the gap get surprised by null or negative A/B results despite compelling offline evidence. Budget for this in your roadmap.

The offline/online gap is not a reason to skip offline evaluation. It is a reason to calibrate your expectations and maintain a two-stage gate: offline evaluation for candidate selection, online experiment for final validation.

The offline/online gap means your test score and your live score are measuring related but different things. A model can win the test and lose the live experiment because the test is a proxy and proxies are imperfect.

cards.title: A/B Testing Fundamentals
cards.teaser: A/B testing is randomized controlled experimentation: split traffic randomly into control and treatment, measure an outcome metric for each group, and use statistics to determine whether the treatment caused the observed difference.

runs.text: An A/B test has five required elements:

items.text: Unit of randomization.
What gets assigned to control or treatment? Usually user ID or session ID. Must be stable (the same user always sees the same variant) and granular enough to provide statistical power.
Control (A).
The current system. The baseline you are trying to beat. Often the model currently in production.
Treatment (B).
The new system. The model or feature change you are evaluating.
Primary metric.

The one metric that decides the experiment's outcome. Committing to this before the experiment runs prevents post-hoc metric shopping. Typical choices: click-through rate, session length, conversion rate, day-7 retention.
Significance criterion.

The threshold that determines whether the observed difference is real or noise. Typically p < 0.05 (5% false positive rate) with 80% statistical power. These must be chosen before the experiment starts.

runs.text: Randomization is the critical design property. It ensures that on average, users assigned to control and treatment are identical in every dimension you did not measure — age, device type, usage pattern, propensity to churn. Without randomization, you are running an observational study, which cannot establish causation.
Common failure modes in A/B test design:

items.text: Novelty effect.
Users interact more with anything new. Short experiments overestimate treatment effect for changes that produce novelty-driven engagement.
Network interference (SUTVA violation).

In social products, a user assigned to treatment can affect users assigned to control (e.g., they see each other's content). Standard A/B testing assumes treatment of one unit does not affect other units.
Instrumentation bias.
Logging the metric differently between control and treatment introduces systematic error that looks like model effect.

runs.text: An A/B test randomly splits your users into two groups, shows each group a different version, measures what happens, and uses statistics to decide if the difference was real or just noise. Randomization is what makes it causal rather than correlational.

cards.title: Sample Size and Statistical Power
cards.teaser: Running an experiment too short gives you noise. Running it too long wastes time and exposes users to a potentially worse experience. Sample-size calculation before the experiment starts is the discipline that prevents both errors.

runs.text: The four quantities that govern experiment duration:

items.text: Minimum detectable effect (MDE).
The smallest treatment difference you care about. If a 0.1% improvement in click-through rate has no business value, your MDE should be higher. Smaller MDE requires more samples.
Baseline metric value.
Current click-through rate, current conversion rate. Higher variance in the baseline metric requires more samples.
Significance level (alpha).
The false positive rate you accept. alpha = 0.05 means you will incorrectly declare a winner 5% of the time when there is no real effect.
Statistical power (1 - beta).
The probability of detecting a real effect when one exists. Power = 0.80 means you will miss a real effect 20% of the time. Higher power requires more samples.

runs.text: The standard sample-size formula for a two-proportion test:
n = 2 * (z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 * p*(1-p) / delta^2

Where p is the baseline conversion rate and delta is the MDE. For a 2% baseline CTR and a 10% relative MDE (detecting a 0.2pp lift), at alpha=0.05 and power=0.80, you need approximately 200,000 users per arm.
Practical guidance from Microsoft's ExP platform (described in "A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls", Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017):

items.text: Run experiments for at least one full week to capture day-of-week effects.
Pre-register your sample size calculation. Stopping early when results look good inflates false positive rates dramatically (peeking problem).
Use variance reduction techniques (CUPED) to reduce the sample needed by conditioning on pre-experiment metrics.

runs.text: Stopping an experiment early because p < 0.05 appeared can inflate the true false positive rate from 5% to over 25%. Sequential testing methods (mSPRT, always-valid inference) are the correct solution for experiments that must be monitored continuously.

Sample size planning answers: "How many users do I need before I can trust the result?" You trade off between the smallest difference worth detecting, your tolerance for false positives, and your tolerance for missing real effects.

cards.title: Interleaving for Ranking Models
cards.teaser: Interleaving tests two ranking models within a single user's result list — instead of splitting users between model A and model B, you blend their ranked outputs together and measure which model's items get more clicks. It requires 100x fewer users than standard A/B testing for the same statistical power.

runs.text: Interleaving was developed at Netflix and Yahoo for evaluating search and recommendation rankers. The core idea: rather than assigning users to model A or model B, generate result lists from both models for every query, then merge them into a single interleaved list and serve it to the user.
Team-draft interleaving algorithm:

explanation.code:
Query Q submitted by user:

Model A ranking:  [a1, a2, a3, a4, a5 ...]
Model B ranking:  [b2, a1, b3, a3, b5 ...]

Team Draft:
  Flip coin -> A picks first
  Round 1: A picks a1 -> list: [a1]        (A-team: {a1})
  Round 2: B picks b2 -> list: [a1, b2]    (B-team: {b2})
  Round 3: A picks a2 -> list: [a1,b2,a2]  (A-team: {a1,a2})
  Round 4: B picks b3 -> list: [..., b3]   (B-team: {b2,b3})
  ...

User clicks on a1 and b3.
  A-team clicks: 1  (a1)
  B-team clicks: 1  (b3)
  Tie -> no preference signal

If user clicks a1 and a2:
  A-team clicks: 2, B-team clicks: 0 -> A wins this query

runs.text: Why interleaving requires fewer samples: in a standard A/B test, differences between users (some users click more, some less) create noise. Interleaving eliminates inter-user noise entirely by showing both models to the same user in the same session. The comparison is within-user, which has much lower variance.

Hofmann et al. (2013) "Reusing Historical Interaction Data for Faster Online Learning" and the Netflix engineering blog post "Interleaving in Online Experiments at Netflix" (2016) both demonstrate 100x efficiency gains over standard A/B testing for ranking evaluation.

items.text: Limitation: interleaving measures which model's items get clicked in a blended list. It does not measure business outcomes like session length, revenue, or day-30 retention. Use interleaving for rapid candidate selection, then confirm with a standard A/B test on business metrics.

runs.text: Interleaving mixes results from two models into one list for each user, then counts which model's items got clicked. Because both models are evaluated by the same users in the same session, you get a much cleaner signal with far fewer users than a standard A/B split.

cards.title: Shadow Traffic
cards.teaser: Shadow traffic runs your new model in parallel with the production model — taking real inputs, generating real predictions, but never serving them to users. It is the safest way to validate a new model's latency, error rate, and output distribution before it touches live traffic.

runs.text: Shadow traffic (also called shadow mode or dark launch) duplicates production requests to a new model endpoint. The new model processes the request in real time, but its response is discarded rather than returned to the user. Production behavior is unchanged.
What shadow traffic validates:

items.text: Latency under real load.
Staging environments do not reproduce the load patterns, cache hit rates, and co-tenancy effects of production. Shadow traffic gives you p50/p99 latency numbers under real conditions.
Error rate.
Null pointer exceptions, deserialization failures, and edge-case inputs that do not appear in your test suite appear in production traffic. Shadow mode catches these before they affect users.
Output distribution shift.

Compare the distribution of scores, class probabilities, or ranked lists from the new model against the old. A dramatic shift in output distribution is a signal that something is wrong, even if the model is not throwing errors.
Resource consumption.
CPU, memory, GPU utilization, downstream API call rates. A model that is 10x more expensive to serve than the champion may not be deployable at scale.

runs.text: Shadow traffic does not tell you whether the model's outputs are better for users — the outputs are never shown, so there is no user feedback signal. It is a validity and reliability check, not an effectiveness check.

Typical shadow traffic pipeline: route 100% of requests to production model + 5-10% to shadow model via a sidecar or traffic duplication proxy. Log shadow responses to a separate store. Compare daily. Graduate to A/B test only after shadow passes SLA checks.
Shadow traffic feeds your new model real production requests, but throws away its answers. You can see if it is slow, crashing, or producing weird outputs without any user ever seeing those outputs.

cards.title: Gradual Rollout
cards.teaser: Gradual rollout is the practice of incrementally shifting traffic from the old model to the new one — 1% to 10% to 50% to 100% — with monitoring gates at each stage. It is the primary mechanism for limiting blast radius when a model change causes harm.

runs.text: Gradual rollout (also called canary deployment for ML models) separates the deployment event from the risk event. The model is deployed to production infrastructure in a single operation, but traffic is shifted incrementally over hours or days.
A standard rollout ladder:

items.text: 1% (canary).
Catch catastrophic failures: hard crashes, timeout spikes, near-zero engagement. Monitor for 2-4 hours. If error rate or latency SLA is breached, rollback immediately.
Enough traffic to observe metric trends. Monitor for 24 hours. Watch primary business metric and guardrail metrics.
This is now a live A/B test. Hold for the pre-calculated experiment duration. Declare winner based on primary metric and guardrail conditions.
Full rollout. Old model remains warm for fast rollback window (typically 48 hours).

runs.text: Guardrail metrics are the key discipline in gradual rollout. Before the rollout begins, define a set of metrics that, if they degrade beyond a threshold, trigger an automatic or policy-mandated rollback regardless of what the primary metric shows. Common guardrails: 5xx error rate, p99 latency, content policy violation rate, critical user journey completion rate.
Rollback must be tested before it is needed. A rollback capability that has never been exercised is a theoretical capability, not an operational one. Practice rolling back in staging under load.

Gradual rollout does not substitute for A/B testing — it is a delivery safety mechanism, not a measurement tool. Running 50/50 traffic as part of the rollout ladder can serve both purposes simultaneously, but only if you planned the experiment design (randomization unit, primary metric, sample size) before starting.

Gradual rollout means you start by sending 1% of users to the new model, check that nothing breaks, then ramp to 10%, 50%, and 100% — with automatic or human-triggered rollback at each step if something goes wrong.

cards.title: Multi-Armed Bandits
cards.teaser: Multi-armed bandits are a family of online algorithms that adaptively allocate traffic to variants based on observed performance, rather than holding allocation fixed for the duration of an experiment. They reduce regret — the cost of serving a suboptimal variant during exploration.

runs.text: In a standard A/B test, you allocate, say, 50% of traffic to each variant for the full experiment duration, regardless of which variant is performing better. If variant B is clearly better after day 3, you still send 50% to the inferior variant A for the remaining 11 days. This is regret: the cumulative cost of not serving the best option during exploration.
Multi-armed bandit algorithms solve the exploration-exploitation tradeoff: allocate more traffic to variants that appear to be winning while continuing to gather information about all variants.
Three widely-used bandit algorithms:

items.text: Epsilon-greedy.

With probability epsilon (e.g., 10%), pick a random variant (explore). With probability 1-epsilon, pick the current best variant (exploit). Simple but suboptimal — it explores uniformly even when some variants are clearly inferior.
UCB (Upper Confidence Bound).

Pick the variant with the highest upper confidence bound on its mean reward. Arms with high uncertainty have high UCB, so exploration targets uncertain arms rather than clearly inferior ones. Provably optimal in the asymptotic regime.
Thompson Sampling.

For each arm, maintain a posterior distribution over its mean reward. At each step, sample from each posterior and pick the arm with the highest sample. Naturally balances exploration and exploitation; works well in practice and is favored by Netflix and Google.

runs.text: Bandits are most appropriate when: the experiment needs to run for a long time, the cost of serving the inferior variant is high (e.g., revenue loss), and you have a relatively simple, single-metric objective.

Bandits are less appropriate when: you need unbiased statistical inference for long-term effect estimation, you have multiple metrics with complex tradeoffs, or you need to detect novelty decay (bandits will re-allocate toward novelty-driven engagement that fades).

A multi-armed bandit is like an A/B test that dynamically routes more traffic to whatever is working. It reduces the cost of running a bad variant, but makes statistical inference harder because allocation becomes dependent on outcomes.

cards.title: Contextual Bandits
cards.teaser: Contextual bandits extend multi-armed bandits with per-request features. Rather than asking "which variant is best overall?", a contextual bandit asks "which variant is best for this user, given their context?" This enables personalization within the experiment itself.

runs.text: A contextual bandit is defined by three components: a context (feature vector describing the current request — user history, device type, time of day), a set of actions (model variants or candidate items), and a reward signal (click, conversion, rating) observed after taking an action.
The bandit learns a policy: a mapping from context to action that maximizes expected reward. Unlike a standard bandit, the optimal action can differ for different users.
Practical algorithm classes:

items.text: LinUCB.

Fits a linear model of reward as a function of context features for each arm. Maintains uncertainty estimates that shrink as more data arrives. Scales to many features. Described in Li et al. (2010), "A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation" (Yahoo).
Neural contextual bandits.
Use a neural network to learn the reward function. More expressive but harder to maintain well-calibrated uncertainty. NeuralUCB and Neural Thompson Sampling are active research areas.
Vowpal Wabbit.
Microsoft's open-source library for contextual bandits. Widely used in production systems. Supports CB exploration, offline evaluation via IPS, and policy gradient methods.

runs.text: The central challenge in contextual bandits is the exploration-exploitation tradeoff at the individual level. The bandit must sometimes choose a suboptimal action for a given user in order to learn whether that action might be optimal for users with similar features.

Contextual bandits are the bridge between A/B testing ("which variant is better?") and full recommendation/ranking ("what should I show this user?"). Netflix uses contextual bandits for artwork selection: the same title may have a different optimal thumbnail for different user segments.

A contextual bandit is a bandit that gets to see who the user is before deciding which arm to pull. It learns that variant A works better for users who prefer action movies and variant B works better for users who prefer documentaries.

cards.title: The Counterfactual Problem
cards.teaser: You can only observe what actually happened — not what would have happened if a different model had served the same request. This fundamental impossibility is the counterfactual problem, and it makes causal evaluation of ML systems hard in ways that are easy to overlook.

runs.text: The counterfactual problem arises from a basic constraint: each user request is served by exactly one model, at one point in time. You observe the outcome for that model. You do not — and cannot — observe the outcome that would have occurred if a different model had served the same request in the same context.

Formally, let Y(a) denote the potential outcome for a request if action a were taken. You observe Y(A_i) for the action actually taken, A_i. For all other actions a != A_i, Y(a) is unobserved. These unobserved outcomes are counterfactuals.
Why this matters in ML:

items.text: Offline evaluation uses historical data logged by a previous policy. If the new model would have served different items, you have no labels for those items. Evaluation on logged data is biased toward the behavior of the logging policy.
Bandit feedback is partial. You only observe reward for the item you showed, not for the items you did not show. Learning from this partial feedback requires counterfactual reasoning.

A/B testing solves the counterfactual problem via randomization. By randomly assigning users to control and treatment, you ensure that on average, the two groups have identical potential outcomes — so the observed difference is causal. But randomization is only available for prospective experiments, not retrospective analysis of logged data.

runs.text: Comparing model A's performance on data logged when model A was deployed versus model B's performance on data logged when model B was deployed is not a valid comparison. The data distributions are different because the policies that generated them were different. This is the counterfactual trap.

The counterfactual problem is that you can only see what happened with the model you actually used, not what would have happened with any other model. A/B testing sidesteps this by randomly splitting users so you get parallel realities at the population level.

cards.title: Counterfactual Evaluation — IPS and Doubly Robust Estimators
cards.teaser: Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) and doubly robust estimators let you evaluate a new policy using data logged by an old policy — the key technique for offline evaluation when online experiments are too expensive or too slow.

runs.text: Counterfactual evaluation (also called off-policy evaluation) estimates how a new policy would have performed on historical data, correcting for the fact that the data was collected under a different policy.
Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS):
IPS_estimate = (1/n) * sum_i [ pi_new(a_i | x_i) / pi_old(a_i | x_i) * r_i ]

Where pi_old is the logging policy's probability of taking action a_i in context x_i, pi_new is the new policy's probability, and r_i is the observed reward. The ratio re-weights each observed outcome by how much more (or less) the new policy would have taken that action.

items.text: IPS is unbiased when the propensity scores are known exactly (as in a randomized logging policy).
IPS has high variance when the new policy deviates substantially from the logging policy (rare actions get extreme weights).
Clipping propensity weights (cap at some maximum value) trades bias for variance reduction.

runs.text: Doubly Robust (DR) estimator combines IPS with a direct model (DM) estimate:
DR = DM_estimate + (1/n) * sum_i [ (pi_new/pi_old) * (r_i - DM_i) ]

The DR estimator is consistent if either the propensity model or the direct model is correctly specified — not necessarily both. It is typically lower-variance than IPS alone. Doubly robust methods are standard in Microsoft's Vowpal Wabbit and in academic counterfactual evaluation literature.

IPS requires that the logging policy has non-zero probability of taking every action the new policy might take — this is the positivity or overlap assumption. If the new policy explores actions the logging policy never took, IPS breaks down. Designing logging policies with deliberate exploration (epsilon-greedy) is what makes counterfactual evaluation feasible.

IPS reweights historical data to correct for the fact that it was collected by a different model. If the old model rarely showed item X but the new model would show it often, IPS upweights the reward signal from those rare X appearances so you get an unbiased estimate of the new model's performance.

cards.title: Lift Hunting and P-Hacking
cards.teaser: Lift hunting is the practice of running an experiment, seeing a null result, and then slicing the data until you find a subgroup that shows improvement. P-hacking is stopping or extending experiments based on observed p-values. Both are anti-patterns that produce false confidence at scale.

runs.text: Statistical significance testing has a known weakness: if you test enough hypotheses, you will find significant results by chance. At alpha=0.05, you expect 1 in 20 true-null hypotheses to appear significant. When experimenters search for significant results post-hoc, they exploit this rate.
Common forms of experimental anti-patterns:

items.text: Metric shopping.
Testing 15 metrics and declaring success when one reaches p < 0.05. If you test 15 independent metrics at alpha=0.05, the probability of at least one spurious positive is 1 - 0.95^15 = 54%.
Subgroup mining.
The overall result is null, so you slice by device, country, user tenure, and browser until a subgroup shows significance. Each slice multiplies your false positive exposure.
Temporal cherry-picking.
The experiment shows significance during week 1 but not week 2. You report the week 1 result. You have now used 2x the data to find 1 significant window.
Optional stopping (peeking).
Checking the p-value daily and stopping the experiment as soon as p < 0.05 is achieved. Under realistic scenarios this can inflate the actual false positive rate from 5% to 40%.

runs.text: Structural solutions:

items.text: Pre-register.

Write down the primary metric, the sample size calculation, and any planned subgroup analyses before the experiment runs. Treat post-hoc discoveries as hypothesis-generating, not hypothesis-confirming.
Multiple testing correction.
Apply Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg corrections when testing multiple metrics.
Sequential testing.
Use always-valid inference methods (mSPRT, e-values) if you need to monitor experiments continuously without inflating false positive rates.

runs.text: Microsoft's ExP (Experimentation Platform) enforces pre-registration at the system level — you must declare your primary metric before the experiment starts, and the platform warns you when you are viewing results before the pre-calculated end date. This is the organizational implementation of anti-p-hacking discipline.

Lift hunting means rummaging through your experiment data until you find something that looks significant. If you look hard enough with enough metrics and slices, you will always find something — but it is usually noise. The fix is to decide what you are measuring before you start, and stick to it.

cards.title: Long-Term vs Short-Term Metrics
cards.teaser: A model change can increase short-term engagement while decreasing long-term retention. The metric you can measure quickly (clicks) and the metric you actually care about (lifetime value, retention, revenue) often diverge — and optimizing the former can actively harm the latter.

runs.text: Online experiments naturally measure short-term metrics: what happens during the experiment window. But many product goals are long-term: will users still be active in 30 days? Will they convert to paid? Will they refer friends?
The taxonomy of metric horizons:

items.text: Immediate metrics (seconds to minutes).
Click-through rate, page load time, scroll depth. High signal-to-noise ratio within hours. Easy to measure. Often poor proxies for long-term value.
Session metrics (minutes to hours).
Session length, tasks completed, queries reformulated. Better proxies for satisfaction than clicks. Measurable within a day.
Short-term retention (days to weeks).
Day-1, Day-7 return rate. Strong predictor of long-term retention. Requires holding the experiment for 1-2 weeks.
Long-term value (months to years).
Day-30 retention, subscription renewal, lifetime value. The metrics you actually want to optimize. Impractical to measure directly in most experiments.

runs.text: The proxy chain problem: companies build metric hierarchies where immediate metrics are validated as proxies for long-term value. The validation itself is expensive — you must run long experiments or observe natural variation over many months to establish that day-7 retention predicts day-90 retention in your product.

Netflix's approach (described in "Experimentation and Measurement for News Feed Ranking"-adjacent work and blog posts) is to maintain a library of validated surrogate metrics: short-term metrics that have been empirically shown to correlate with long-term retention in their specific product context. Crucially, a metric that is a valid surrogate for product A may not be a valid surrogate for product B.

Metric toxicity: some changes increase immediate engagement by being annoying or alarming (clickbait, false urgency). These show strong short-term metric gains while causing long-term user burnout and churn. Guardrail metrics on user sentiment, complaint rates, and unsubscribe rates exist specifically to catch metric-toxic changes.

Every metric is gameable. A team that is evaluated purely on click-through rate will eventually build a model that generates high click-through rates at the expense of satisfaction, trust, and retention. Metric design is not a technical problem — it is a product strategy problem.

Short-term metrics are easy to measure but can be misleading. Clicks go up, users come back less. The fix is to validate that your short-term proxy metrics actually predict the long-term outcomes you care about — and check that whenever you improve the proxy, the long-term metric eventually follows.

cards.title: Experiment Taxonomy — When to Use What
cards.teaser: Shadow traffic, interleaving, standard A/B tests, bandits, and counterfactual evaluation are not interchangeable — each occupies a specific place in the model evaluation lifecycle, with different costs, different statistical properties, and different appropriate uses.

runs.text: A mature ML team maintains a portfolio of evaluation techniques and chooses among them based on the evaluation goal, available traffic volume, experiment duration tolerance, and statistical requirements.

items.text: Offline evaluation.
Use for: rapid candidate selection among many model variants. Cost: engineering time. Limitation: offline/online gap; cannot measure user behavior causally.
Counterfactual evaluation (IPS/DR).
Use for: offline estimation of online performance when A/B tests are too slow or too expensive. Requires logged propensity scores. Limitation: bias if logging policy has low overlap with new policy.
Shadow traffic.
Use for: pre-launch reliability, latency, and output distribution validation. No user impact. Limitation: cannot measure whether model outputs are better for users.
Interleaving.

Use for: fast relative ranking of two ranker models on click preference. 100x more sample-efficient than A/B. Limitation: measures click preference only; does not measure business outcomes or long-term metrics.
Standard A/B test.

Use for: definitive causal measurement of a model change's effect on primary business metrics. Gold standard for causal inference. Limitation: requires large sample sizes and experiment duration; measures average treatment effect.
Multi-armed / contextual bandit.
Use for: adaptive optimization when minimizing regret matters more than inference. Also for personalization. Limitation: complicates statistical inference; novelty decay not handled gracefully.

runs.text: A typical model evaluation pipeline combines these techniques in sequence: offline evaluation eliminates weak candidates, counterfactual evaluation narrows the field further, shadow traffic validates reliability, interleaving ranks surviving candidates quickly, and a full A/B test on the final candidate measures business impact before full rollout.

Different evaluation methods answer different questions at different costs. Use offline evaluation to filter, shadow traffic to de-risk, interleaving to compare rankers cheaply, and A/B testing to measure business impact. They are a pipeline, not alternatives.

cards.title: The Experimentation Platform as Infrastructure
cards.teaser: At scale, A/B testing is not an ad-hoc activity — it is infrastructure. Companies like Microsoft (ExP), Netflix (Experimentation Platform), and Airbnb (Experistat) have built internal platforms that handle randomization, metric computation, statistical testing, and experiment lifecycle management.

runs.text: When an organization runs hundreds of concurrent experiments, managing them by hand creates systematic problems: traffic splits conflict, experiments interact, statistical analyses are rerun inconsistently, and results are stored in spreadsheets. An experimentation platform solves these at the infrastructure level.
Core capabilities of a mature experimentation platform:

items.text: Randomization service.
Deterministic hash-based assignment: given (user_id, experiment_id), return the assigned variant consistently. Ensures the same user always sees the same variant, even across sessions and devices.
Namespace and layer management.

Organizes experiments into layers so that multiple experiments can run simultaneously without interfering with each other's randomization. A user can be in experiment X and experiment Y simultaneously, in orthogonal traffic partitions.
Metric computation pipeline.
Joins experiment assignment logs with behavioral event logs to compute per-user metric values for each experiment variant. Automated, auditable, reproducible.
Statistical testing engine.
Applies consistent statistical tests (t-test, Mann-Whitney, CUPED variance reduction) across all experiments. Prevents bespoke re-analysis.
Pre-registration enforcement.
Forces teams to declare primary metric and sample size before launch. Flags peeking behavior.

runs.text: Microsoft's ExP platform, described in "Overlapping Experiment Infrastructure: More, Better, Faster Experimentation" (Tang et al., KDD 2010) and "A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls" (Dmitriev et al., KDD 2017), processes thousands of concurrent experiments across Microsoft's products and has become a reference architecture for large-scale experimentation.

Open-source options for teams building internal platforms: GrowthBook (metrics + statistical engine), Flagr (feature flags + experiment assignment), and the statsig SDK (assignment + metric computation). At early stage, a well-governed spreadsheet of pre-registered experiments plus a shared Jupyter notebook for analysis is a better starting point than building a platform prematurely.

An experimentation platform is the infrastructure that makes running many experiments simultaneously safe and rigorous — consistent randomization, automated metric computation, and guardrails against p-hacking, all managed centrally rather than by each team independently.
